title: Cannabis-Specific Workplace Exposures and Emergency Escalation

content.overview: Cannabis work can involve respiratory, allergic, chemical, gas, physical, ergonomic and biological exposures. Learners practice recognizing meaningful patterns, checking whether controls are functioning, documenting facts, and choosing routine, stop-work, medical-reporting or emergency escalation without attempting self-diagnosis.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which exposure can lead the immune system to react to a substance; reactions may develop after repeated exposure and vary between workers.
Airborne plant-derived dust or particles that can contribute to irritation or allergic exposure.
A factual relationship between symptoms and work timing, task, location or exposure conditions that should be reported and evaluated rather than self-diagnosed.
Transfer of a condition to a person or team with the authority and competence to manage it.

sections.title: Recognize the exposure landscape
sections.body: NIOSH identifies cannabis-industry exposures that can include carbon dioxide, ozone, pesticides, volatile organic compounds, plant allergens, microbes, endotoxins, organic particulate, heat, noise, ultraviolet light, repetitive work and general safety hazards. The actual risk depends on the task, process and workplace controls, so technicians observe the real work condition rather than treating cultivation as one uniform exposure profile.

sections.title: Work-related respiratory patterns deserve early reporting
sections.body: NIOSH reports that cannabis cultivation and processing workers can experience work-related asthma and allergic or irritant symptoms. Symptoms may develop after repeated exposure and may improve away from work. A technician's job is to report the pattern, task and control condition accurately and seek the workplace or medical evaluation pathway—not to diagnose the cause personally.

sections.title: Control failures matter as much as exposure names
sections.body: A visible dust cloud, failed local control, damaged enclosure, missing ventilation, unverified chemical identity or active gas alarm can change the response even before anyone knows the exact exposure concentration. Technician I workers use the assessed controls, stop or leave the area when the procedure requires it, and escalate control failures to the responsible role.

workedExamples: Recurring coughing or chest tightness associated with one dusty task is reported with the task and timing pattern instead of being dismissed because symptoms improve later.
A CO2 life-safety alarm triggers the posted emergency procedure rather than an unauthorized room entry to inspect the controller.
Visible plant dust increases while assigned local exhaust is not operating, so the task is paused and the failed control is escalated rather than compensated for by working faster.

A worker reports skin and eye irritation after repeated handling work; the technician documents the task and control conditions and routes the concern through the workplace health and safety process without labeling it as a specific allergy.
commonMistakes: Assuming natural plant material cannot contribute to occupational allergy, irritation or asthma.
Treating a symptom report as proof of a specific diagnosis instead of a signal for qualified evaluation.
Relying on any available mask or extra PPE when an engineering or process control has failed.
Entering an alarmed or potentially unsafe space to investigate without assigned emergency-response authority.
Recording vague statements such as 'felt bad around plants' without the task, time, location or control condition needed to understand the pattern.
content.practicalApplication: Review a set of cultivation exposure cases and decide whether the immediate response is continue with verified controls, pause/correct, stop/escalate, follow the workplace symptom-reporting pathway, or initiate the posted emergency response. For symptom cases, document the factual task/time pattern without diagnosing the worker.
content.summary: Cannabis-specific safety competence means recognizing meaningful exposure conditions and symptom patterns, verifying that controls are functioning, documenting facts clearly, and escalating early. Technicians do not self-diagnose respiratory or allergic disease and do not improvise entry into alarmed areas.

blocks.title: Natural does not mean nonhazardous
blocks.body: Cannabis plant material and cultivation work can involve organic particulate, allergens, microbes, pesticides, carbon dioxide, ozone, heat, noise, ultraviolet light, repetitive work and other facility-specific exposures. The presence and level of risk vary by task and workplace, so site-specific assessment and controls matter.

blocks.alt: Simplified cultivation room showing irrigation water approaching damaged electrical equipment, a blocked aisle, an unstable ladder, an exposed cutting tool, high-intensity lighting, and a carbon-dioxide life-safety alarm, with a reminder to scan for other task-specific exposures.
blocks.caption: A visual room scan should include ordinary workplace hazards and exposures that can be prominent in cultivation work.

blocks.title: Exposure categories and the first Technician I question
rows: Plant dust, organic particulate, allergens, microbes
Are the assessed source/engineering/work-practice controls functioning, and is anyone reporting a work-related symptom pattern?
Cleaning chemicals, pesticides where applicable, ozone or other process chemicals
Can the exact product and current controls be verified from the label/SDS and procedure?
Heat, intense light/UV, noise, slips, falls, ladders
Can the condition be controlled safely within the approved routine procedure?
Carbon-dioxide enrichment or other monitored gas conditions
Is an alarm or posted emergency condition active? If so, follow the emergency procedure rather than entering to investigate.
Repetitive hand work, awkward handling, material movement
Are approved work methods and aids adequate, and are symptoms or task demands changing?
Mold, fungi, endotoxin and other microbial material
Are sanitation, moisture, ventilation and task-specific controls functioning as intended?

items.title: Protect immediate safety
items.body: If the person is in distress or the area is under an emergency condition, use the site's emergency response process and obtain appropriate medical help.

items.title: Record the pattern, not a diagnosis
items.body: Capture the task, location, approximate timing, observed conditions, control status and the worker-reported symptoms using the workplace process.

items.title: Check the control condition
items.body: Note whether ventilation, local controls, enclosure, housekeeping or required PPE was operating and used as assigned.

items.title: Report through the workplace pathway
items.body: Notify the designated supervisor, safety/health function or other responsible role as required by policy.

items.title: Support qualified evaluation
items.body: Medical diagnosis and decisions about individual health restrictions belong to qualified healthcare professionals and the employer's established program.

blocks.title: Early recognition matters
blocks.body: NIOSH emphasizes early recognition of work-related asthma and reduction or elimination of causative workplace exposure where possible. A technician can contribute by reporting patterns early and accurately instead of normalizing symptoms or waiting for them to become severe.

blocks.title: Report patterns; do not self-diagnose
blocks.body: Recurring cough, wheeze, chest tightness, shortness of breath, eye irritation, skin reactions or other symptoms associated with work should be reported through the workplace health and safety process. Medical diagnosis belongs to qualified health professionals.

blocks.title: Symptoms during one dusty task
blocks.setting: A worker reports coughing and chest tightness that repeatedly appear during one dusty dry-plant handling task and improve after leaving that work area. A coworker suggests grabbing any available dust mask and continuing.
blocks.prompt: What is the stronger Technician I response?
options: Continue because the symptoms improve later
Use any available mask without checking the program
Report the work-related symptom pattern, document the task/control conditions, and verify the assessed controls and required PPE before the task resumes
Move faster so exposure time is shorter
blocks.answer: Report the work-related symptom pattern, document the task/control conditions, and verify the assessed controls and required PPE before the task resumes.
blocks.feedback: A repeatable relationship between symptoms and work is important information. It should be reported and evaluated, while the workplace controls for the task are checked. The technician should not diagnose asthma or improvise respiratory protection.

blocks.title: The control failed before symptoms occurred
blocks.setting: A dry-processing task begins normally. During the shift, visible plant dust increases and the assigned local control stops operating. No one has reported symptoms yet.
options: Pause the task and follow the procedure for the failed exposure control rather than relying on symptoms as the trigger
Open nearby doors without authorization and keep working
Give everyone extra disposable masks and continue
blocks.answer: Pause the task and follow the procedure for the failed exposure control rather than relying on symptoms as the trigger.
blocks.feedback: Control failure is itself actionable. Waiting for symptoms is not an adequate exposure-control strategy, and improvised PPE does not replace the assessed control system.

blocks.title: Alarms are action signals, not diagnosis invitations
blocks.body: A carbon-dioxide or other life-safety alarm should trigger the posted response procedure. If you are not assigned emergency-response duties, do not enter an unsafe or alarmed area simply to check a controller or see whether the condition feels normal.

blocks.title: Work-related symptom pattern note
blocks.description: A factual pattern note helps the designated safety/health or medical process understand what happened without turning the technician into the diagnostician.

fields.label: Worker-reported symptom
fields.value: Use the worker's own factual description; do not assign a diagnosis

fields.label: Task and material
fields.value: What work was being performed and what materials/processes were involved

fields.label: Timing / pattern
fields.value: When symptoms occurred in relation to the task and whether they changed away from the work exposure

fields.label: Control status
fields.value: Whether assigned ventilation, local controls, enclosure, housekeeping and required PPE were functioning/used

fields.label: Immediate action
fields.value: Pause, stop-work, emergency action, supervisor notification or other step taken under procedure

fields.label: Escalation
fields.value: Safety/health, supervisor, medical or other responsible role notified under the employer's process

blocks.note: This is a training model for factual reporting, not a medical record or diagnosis form.

blocks.title: Exposure, symptom-pattern and escalation sort
blocks.instructions: Classify each case as continue with verified controls, pause/correct, stop/escalate, workplace symptom reporting, or emergency response. Record the observation that drove the classification and the facts that should be handed off.
prompts: Plant dust is visible during a task and the assigned local-control equipment is not operating.
A life-safety gas alarm activates in an enriched room.
A worker reports repeated skin irritation associated with one handling task.
A worker reports cough and chest tightness that recur during a dusty task and improve away from work.
A chemical container is present but the product identity cannot be confirmed.
A repetitive task causes increasing hand discomfort across the shift even though the worker is meeting production targets.
blocks.artifact: Exposure-escalation decision sheet plus one completed symptom-pattern note

blocks.title: Remediation cue
blocks.body: If your response waits for severe symptoms, assumes 'natural' means safe, treats any mask as an adequate fix, or names a medical diagnosis from a symptom report, revise the decision. Technician I performance is about early recognition, verified controls, factual reporting and correct escalation.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Cultivation-specific competence is not memorizing a list of hazards. It is recognizing meaningful exposure conditions and work-related symptom patterns early, verifying that controls are functioning, documenting facts without overclaiming, and selecting the correct escalation or emergency route when routine work is no longer controlled.
